An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows

Abstract
AI agents depend on repeated decisions to ac-
complish tasks, with large language models
(LLMs) commonly serving as their core de-
cision makers. The recent emergence of Jev
offers an opportunity to make these decisions
faster and at lower cost. However, it remains
unclear whether such local savings can be trans-
lated into efficient and reliable task comple-
tion. In this paper, we investigate this effi-
ciency transfer across five agents in two repre-
sentative application settings, embodied tasks
in ALFWorld and mobile app use in Android-
World. Across 4,500 task executions, we jointly
evaluate task effectiveness, decision-level and
task-level resource use, and execution behavior.
Experimental results show that Jev integration
substantially reduces decision cost and latency
across all five agents, with task-level gains vary-
ing by workflow. Task success remains close
to baseline levels on ALFWorld and declines
more substantially in two mobile agents. Aux-
iliary reasoning and additional interactions ab-
sorb decision savings, while failed recovery and
premature completion limit successful delivery.
Mean cost per successful outcome increases in
one agent even as spending per attempt falls.
These findings highlight the importance of pre-
serving progress, supporting recovery, and ver-
ifying completion when integrating efficient
decision models into agent workflows. Their
practical value should be assessed through suc-
cessful task delivery, recovery behavior, and
resources per delivered outcome.
1 Introduction
AI agents pursue goals through interaction with
their environments, with LLMs supporting this
process in different scenarios (Yang et al., 2024;
Wen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Progress
toward a goal depends on repeatedly interpreting
observations and deciding what to do next (Yao
et al., 2023). Some decisions require open-ended
code or text generation, while others involve se-
lecting among available tools, interface elements,
or admissible commands (Wang et al., 2024; Wen
et al., 2024; Shridhar et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2025).
These bounded choices are repeated throughout a
task, and make both action-selection quality and
resource efficiency important to overall agent per-
formance (Kapoor et al., 2025).
The resources spent on these decisions should
reflect their reasoning demands. On S1-Bench,
Zhang et al. (2026b) find that large reasoning mod-
els can overthink simple questions while still mak-
ing errors, showing that extended reasoning does
not consistently yield accurate, economical judg-
ments. This finding motivates examining models
designed for focused decisions. Jev, recently re-
leased by TypeSafe AI as aSystem One Model,
provides instruction-defined judgments through
typed outputs, including probabilities over supplied
choices (Almeida, 2026; TypeSafe AI, 2026b). The
company positions it as a fast, inexpensive decision
model (Almeida, 2026). Its choice interface offers
an opportunity to reduce the cost and latency of re-
peated action selection in AI agents. Whether these
local savings translate into efficient and reliable
task completion remains unclear.
Answering this question requires following de-
cisions through complete agent workflows. Ac-
tions shape subsequent observations and choices,
so each decision affects the conditions for the next
(Ross et al., 2011). An executable action can
move an agent away from its goal, requiring fur-
ther reasoning or recovery whose cost may offset
local savings. Reflection extends these dependen-
cies across attempts (Shinn et al., 2023), and can-
didate construction shapes the choices available
to the decision model (Yang et al., 2024). Task
efficiency therefore depends on auxiliary reason-
ing, interaction overhead, and the sequence of ac-
tions performed. Failed attempts also consume re-
sources without delivering the requested outcome.

Evaluating agent performance requires connecting
decision-level savings to task success, overall re-
source use, and resources per successful outcome,
supported by repeated evaluation and execution
analysis (Kapoor et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025).
To provide this evidence, we conduct a compar-
ative empirical study of AI agents with Jev-based
action selection. The study covers five agent fami-
lies in two representative application settings, em-
bodied tasks in ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021)
and mobile app use in AndroidWorld (Rawles et al.,
2025). Within each family, we compare the original
configuration with a Jev-integrated variant, using
text-only observations to match Jev’s supported
inputs (TypeSafe AI, 2026a). Each configuration
runs three times on the same tasks, yielding 4,500
task executions. We jointly evaluate task effec-
tiveness, decision-level and task-level resource use,
and execution behavior. Paired task-level analyses
estimate uncertainty in the observed differences,
while systematic trace coding characterizes fail-
ure and recovery patterns. Comparisons with the
original configurations assess integration effects.
Our results show that Jev substantially reduces
decision cost and latency across all five agents,
with task-level gains varying by workflow. Task
success remains close to baseline levels on ALF-
World and declines more substantially in two mo-
bile agents. Mean task costs fall across all agents,
while auxiliary reasoning and additional interac-
tions limit overall speed gains. Failed recovery
and premature completion further constrain suc-
cessful delivery. Lower spending per attempt can
therefore coexist with higher cost per successful
outcome. These findings highlight the importance
of preserving progress, supporting recovery, and
verifying completion when integrating efficient de-
cision models into agent workflows. Their practical
value should be assessed through successful task
delivery and the resources it requires. In summary,
we make the following contributions:
• We provide an empirical study of AI agents
with Jev-based action selection across five
agent families and two benchmarks, covering
4,500 task executions.
• We characterize how decision-level savings
translate into task cost, latency, and resources
per successful outcome across workflows.
• We systematically annotate execution traces
and analyze recovery outcomes to identify fail-
ure and recovery patterns.

2 Background
Jev.TypeSafe AI introduced Jev in September
2026 as aSystem One Modelfor fast, structured
decisions in software automation (Almeida, 2026).
Its API maps a shared state and instruction-defined
questions to typed choices, scores, or binary prob-
abilities. Questions are evaluated independently,
and choice questions return probabilities over sup-
plied candidates (TypeSafe AI, 2026b). Entailment-
based classifiers and GLiClass support labels sup-
plied at inference time (Yin et al., 2019; Stepanov
et al., 2025). Jev’s choice interface accepts candi-
date descriptions and instructions that define the
decision to make. An agent can supply its goal,
observations, and available actions as context for
each selection. This connects the typed interface
to repeated decisions within a workflow. Early Jev
studies examine probabilistic coding of crash nar-
ratives (Rafe and Das, 2026) and adoption across
public software projects (Ling et al., 2026). We
examine how its structured decisions interact with
reasoning, environment feedback, and repeated ac-
tion selection during task execution.
3 Related Work
Agent Action Selection.LLM agents repeatedly
map goals, observations, and interaction history to
actions through reasoning and environment inter-
action (Yao et al., 2023). Their interfaces expose
commands, UI operations, and tools across em-
bodied, mobile, and software tasks (Wang et al.,
2024; Wen et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). Tool use
requires deciding which APIs to invoke, when to
call them, and which arguments to supply (Schick
et al., 2023). A finite set of action types can still re-
quire open-ended arguments, so bounded selection
and generation coexist within one agent. The sur-
rounding workflow determines which candidates
are available and how the selected action is exe-
cuted. Feedback, reflection, and memory condition
later decisions on earlier outcomes (Shinn et al.,
2023; Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026). We
focus on the bounded-selection component, exam-
ining how a specialized decision model interacts
with the workflow’s reasoning, environment inter-
action, and recovery mechanisms.
Efficient Decision Models and Routing.Rout-
ing and cascades assign requests across models

using difficulty, preferences, or confidence to bal-
ance cost and response quality (Ding et al., 2024;
Ong et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025). Agent systems
extend model allocation to collaboration modes
and roles through MasRouter (Yue et al., 2025).
EvoRoute uses experience and environment feed-
back for step-level backbone selection, evaluat-
ing performance, cost, and latency (Zhang et al.,
2026a). These methods optimize which model a
system invokes. We study specialized bounded
action selection across five agent families, char-
acterizing when decision-level savings transfer to
task-level efficiency considering auxiliary reason-
ing, interaction length, recovery, and completion.
Agent Evaluation and Sequential Reliabil-
ity.Benchmarks assess task outcomes across
embodied, web, mobile, desktop, and software-
engineering environments (Shridhar et al., 2021;
Zhou et al., 2024b; Rawles et al., 2025; Xie et al.,
2024; Jimenez et al., 2024). ALFWorld and An-
droidWorld provide the outcomes for our house-
hold and mobile evaluations. Resource-aware eval-
uation considers accuracy and expenditure, while
repeated trials assess consistency (Kapoor et al.,
2025; Yao et al., 2025). Sequential errors can com-
pound as earlier decisions alter the states encoun-
tered later (Ross et al., 2011). Feedback, reflection,
and tree search support correction across attempts
or alternative action paths (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhou
et al., 2024a). Failure analysis identifies difficul-
ties in long-term reasoning, decision-making, and
instruction following (Liu et al., 2024). Trajectory
diagnosis evaluates backtracking, observation read-
ing, and self-verification in web agents (Ou et al.,
2025). We connect decision-level resources to total
expenditure and resources per delivered success, in-
cluding failed attempts, and characterize recovery
and completion errors through trace coding.
4 Empirical Study Design
Selecting among finite candidates matches Jev’s
stated focus on bounded judgments (TypeSafe AI,
2026b). We therefore assess the benefits and limita-
tions of Jev integration through task effectiveness,
execution efficiency, inference cost, and consis-
tency across runs, examining how decision-level
savings translate into successful task delivery.
4.1 Research Questions
RQ1: Effectiveness.How does integrating Jev
into LLM-based agents affect task success relative
to their original configurations?
RQ2: Efficiency Transfer.When do decision-
level efficiency gains transfer to the overall task-
level efficiency?
RQ3: Failure and Recovery.What failure pat-
terns and recovery behaviors characterize agents
with Jev-based action selection?

4.3 Evaluation and Metrics
Repeated Runs and Aggregation.To capture
consistency and variability in agent execution, we
evaluate each agent configuration three times on
the same tasks, resetting environment state and
agent memory between runs. We retain all task–
run records and report the mean and sample stan-
dard deviation of each metric across runs. Paired
analyses preserve task correspondence. We report
Jminus control differences with 95% task-cluster
bootstrap intervals, resampling tasks and retaining
their three runs together in 20,000 replicates. See
Appendix A.2 for details.
Effectiveness.Our primary metric is task suc-
cess rate, the proportion of tasks completed success-
fully according to the benchmark’s official evalua-
tor. For AndroidWorld, we additionally report the
official task score to capture partial completion.
Efficiency and Cost.We measure token usage,
inference cost, and elapsed time at both task and
decision levels. Task-level token usage and cost
include all model calls, including auxiliary gener-
ation and reflection, while decision-level metrics
cover only action-selection calls. Inference costs
are calculated using fixed model-specific input and
output token prices. We report each metric over
all tasks and over successful tasks only, with the
latter including only decisions from successful ex-
ecutions. Task-level means divide the correspond-
ing totals by the number of tasks, and decision-
level means divide them by the number of action-
selection calls within each scope. We also report
cost and time per delivered success by dividing the
corresponding totals across all attempts, including
failures, by the number of successful executions.

Errors become failures through termination
or failed recovery.Trajectories connect these task
differences to goal interpretation and correction. In
the Wi-Fi task, Jev selects an ambiguously labeled
switch and declares completion with the goal un-
met. This terminal judgment ends the opportunity
for correction. In ALFWorld, selecting a hand-
towel for a cloth leads the workflow to continue
reasoning on the wrong object. The initial error is
amplified as the agent repeatedly preserves the mis-
taken premise. These cases show how a decisive
stopping error can end a short task, while an earlier
selection error can develop into sustained failure
through unsuccessful correction. Reflexion demon-
strates recovery’s contribution at the task level, as
Jev’s first-trial success advantage becomes a final
deficit after further trials (Table 4). Its selection
and auxiliary LLM reflection jointly determine this
outcome. Effective decision making consequently
requires both selecting a goal-appropriate action
and revising previous choices when feedback re-
veals a mismatch.
Jev suits clearly specified decision roles.Jev
is most promising when the decision input makes
the goal, current state, and action prerequisites ex-
plicit, so selecting an action maps an understood
state to a suitable next operation. Promising appli-
cations include workflow routing, API or tool selec-
tion, and routine software operations with identifi-
able targets and observable completion conditions.
Workflows involving ambiguous goals, incomplete
observations, or repeated sub-goal revision place
greater demands on interpretation and recovery,
the capabilities implicated in the observed mobile
deficits. The effectiveness trade-off is strong execu-
tion within well-specified states versus adaptability
when the agent must revise its understanding of the
task. The strongest candidates for Jev have explicit
conditions for choosing, checking, and completing
an action.

5.3 RQ3: Failure and Recovery
To connect task outcomes with agent behavior, we
compare three groups over three runs on fixed tasks,
persistent Jev failures with consistent baseline suc-
cess, the reverse contrast, and mixed outcomes
where each configuration succeeds once or twice.
They contain nineteen, three, and 21 of the 616
family–task pairs (Figure 5), totaling 43 pairs and
258 executions. Figure 6 places them within the

6 Discussion
Model development.Our findings point toward
decision models trained for the consequences of
sequential choices. Jev’s fast selection coexists
with errors in target interpretation, correction, and
termination, and these errors can consume its re-
source savings through prolonged execution. For
Jev and Jev-like models, a promising direction is
to retain concise numerical outputs while strength-
ening sensitivity to goals, action prerequisites, and
contradictory feedback. Training on contrasting
successful and failed trajectories could target deci-
sions that restore progress or correctly end a task.
Another useful objective is calibrated confidence
in whether any available action advances the goal,
giving the model a basis for requesting more in-
formation or reconsidering its choices. Progress
should be assessed through successful task delivery
and the resources it requires, alongside decision
accuracy and response time.
Agentic system design.The engineering impli-
cation is to treat decision making as an explicit
system component with observable inputs, out-
comes, and costs. Candidate interfaces should ex-
pose target identity, prerequisites, and expected
state changes, with feedback indicating whether
the last action advanced the goal. Checks should
focus on completion judgments and repeated lack
of progress, the points where our traces show fail-
ures becoming terminal or persistent. Additional
observation or reasoning can then be directed to
unresolved decisions. This allocation matters be-
cause auxiliary calls and interaction overhead can
absorb the savings from faster selection. Deploy-
ment decisions should jointly consider the original
runtime bottleneck, changes in interaction length,
and expenditure per successful outcome. Jev and
Jev-like models are consequently most promising
in systems that make routine choices inexpensive
while concentrating verification and recovery on
decisions that threaten completion.
7 Conclusion
We evaluate AI agents with Jev-based action se-
lection to examine whether faster, cheaper deci-
sions translate into efficient and reliable task com-
pletion. Across five agents over two scenarios,
decision savings yield workflow-dependent task
gains. Success remains close to baseline on ALF-
World and falls more substantially in two mobile
agents. Auxiliary reasoning and additional inter-
actions absorb savings, while failed recovery and
premature completion limit delivery. Mean cost per
successful outcome rises in one agent despite lower
spending per attempt. Agent workflows should pre-
serve progress, support recovery, and verify com-
pletion. Efficient decision models should be as-
sessed through successful delivery, recovery behav-
ior, and resources per delivered outcome.

Limitations
Evaluation scope.This study examines Jev in-
tegration in selected agent families across mo-
bile application and household-task environments.
Both settings use language-based observations and
bounded action interfaces. Transfer to visually
grounded agents, open-ended tool creation, and
longer workflows requires further evaluation. The
three repetitions characterize execution variability
on fixed task instances with a shared seed. They
do not measure variation across newly sampled
environments or task distributions.
System-level comparisons.Jev operates within
an agent workflow whose candidate construction,
auxiliary generation, and feedback mechanisms
jointly influence performance. Our comparisons
therefore concern the evaluated integrations. The
ALFWorld LLM-Choice control helps distinguish
decision-model effects under a shared candidate
interface, but this control does not cover every
integration. Within-family budget matching sup-
ports comparisons between variants. Comparisons
across families also reflect differences in interac-
tion budgets and workflow design. The findings
should consequently be interpreted in the context
of these configurations, without attributing every
observed difference to Jev alone.
Measurement conditions.Latency and cost
depend on the evaluated model versions, service
conditions, and experimental prices. Hosted infer-
ence introduces variation beyond the agent’s con-
trol, while future model updates or pricing changes
may alter the observed trade-offs. Our account-
ing includes auxiliary model use and failed tasks,
but retry adjustments and imputed usage introduce
measurement uncertainty where applicable. The
reported costs represent estimates under the stated
accounting rules, and timing comparisons retain
the measurement boundaries of each benchmark.

Persistent Jev gains.
All three reverse pairs belong to FastAgent, in-
volving recipe creation, activity-duration reporting,
and adding a map favorite. They expose distinct
contributions from interaction granularity, response
format, and the evaluator’s acceptance criterion.
This reverse contrast connects goal-appropriate
choices with current-state execution and delivery
in the requested response format.
In recipe creation, the first baseline run batches
field operations and reports that a value entered the
wrong field after the form shifted. Jev completes
the task through single-tool steps with updated ob-
servations between operations, keeping choices
grounded in the current layout. For the activity
query, both workflows obtain 105 minutes in run 1.
Jev returns the requested integer “105”, while the
baseline returns a sentence containing that value
and fails the evaluator. Correct calculation and
compliant output are separate requirements. In the
map task, the first baseline run expands its search
and stops when it cannot verify the location. Jev
creates the requested named favorite and passes the
name-based evaluator. This contrast separates ge-
ographic verification from benchmark acceptance.
Successful delivery depends on execution, response
format, and completion criteria.
Mixed outcomes.
The 21 mixed pairs comprise one ReAct, ten
T3A, four AutoDroid, and six FastAgent tasks.
Twenty occur in AndroidWorld. Fixed task in-
stances make these contrasts informative about vari-
ation within the same workflow. Representative
runs differ in prerequisite management and search
strategy, showing inconsistent application of effec-
tive plans.
In two-object placement (ALFWorld 133),
ReAct-Jsucceeds twice andReAct-Bonce. The
failed Jev run holds the first object while repeat-
edly reasoning about collecting the second, whose
inventory prerequisite is unmet. Successful runs
deposit the first object before collecting the next.
Progress requires making a needed action available
as well as choosing among currently admissible
actions. In recipe deletion among irrelevant entries,
both FastAgent variants succeed twice. The failed
Jev run deletes two targets and scrolls for the third
until its budget expires. Successful Jev runs locate

the targets through search, showing that strategy
choice varies within the same configuration.
Action positions.In ALFWorld 046,ReAct-
Brun 2 takes the handtowel at step 3. Cleaning
attempts at steps 5 and 12 return “Nothing hap-
pens”. It deposits the handtowel at step 28, re-
trieves cloth 2 at step 32, cleans it at step 34, and
places it in the cabinet at step 36. In the addi-
tional cup-heating example, ALFWorld 101,ReAct-
Jrun 1 refers to mug 2 as the requested cup and
continues making completion assertions through
step 49. In recipe deletion with irrelevant entries,
FastAgent-Jrun 2 performs 24 swipes after delet-
ing two targets and ends with the third target still
present.
Completion fields and evaluator outcomes.
For the activity-duration query in run 1, the Jev
workflow’s completion call carries the message
“105” with its internal success field set to false.
The returned answer is “105” and receives official
success. For the map-favorite instance, the eval-
uator accepts the stored favorite by its requested
name. The geographic verification attempted by the
baseline is separate from this acceptance condition.
Feedback and completion checks.Across
these cases, reliability hinges on observations
changing consequential choices. Object mis-
matches require revised targets, changing forms
require updated action references, and stalled
progress calls for another strategy. Reflection that
preserves a wrong premise adds little corrective
value, while accepting an unverified goal ends exe-
cution prematurely. Together with the distinction
between real-world verification and benchmark ac-
ceptance, these findings favor checks tied to target
identity, prerequisites, and the requested final state.
